o: A laser starts at the southwest corner of a square room of side p, moving up-and-right so it first hits the east wall at height q. It bounces off mirrored walls; we must report which of the three receptors (0 = southwest... actually 0 is the corner it started from on the left wall at the bottom, 1 = top-left, 2 = top-right) it hits first. The classic trick is to *unfold* the mirrors: instead of reflecting the ray, reflect the room, so the ray travels in a straight line through a grid of p-by-p squares. The ray's path is y = (q/p)·x; it reaches a corner when x and y are both multiples of p, i.e., after L = lcm(p, q) horizontal distance. At that point the ray has crossed L/p squares horizontally and L/q vertically. In example 1 (p=2, q=1), L=2: one square across, two up — an odd number of vertical crossings means it ends on the top edge, and since L/p = 1 is odd it lands on the right wall's top corner, receptor 2. In example 2 (p=3, q=1), L=3: odd across, odd up → receptor 1 (top-left). Constraints are tiny (≤1000), so even a step-by-step reflection simulation works, but the LCM/parity solution is O(log p).
k: Unfold reflections: a bouncing ray in mirrored boxes equals a straight line through copies of the room.
The ray hits a corner exactly at distance lcm(p, q); parity of the number of room-widths and room-heights traveled determines which receptor.
Reduce q/p to lowest terms first (divide by gcd): then m = p/g vertical steps and n = q/g horizontal steps decide the answer by parity.

a.i: Track the ray segment by segment. Each time it hits a wall, flip the appropriate direction component and check whether the hit point is a receptor corner. Since p, q ≤ 1000 and the ray meets a receptor within lcm(p,q)/q ≤ 1000 bounces, this terminates quickly.
s: Start at position (0,0) moving right and up.
Compute where the ray next hits a wall: if moving right, it hits the east wall after (p - x)·(p/q)... more simply advance in unit steps scaled by q vertically per p horizontally.
At each wall contact, record position; if it is a corner (x==0 or x==p combined with y==0 or y==p), return the corresponding receptor number.
Otherwise flip dx or dy depending on which wall was hit and continue.
a.t: O(lcm(p,q)/p) ≤ O(q/gcd) ≤ O(1000) — at most about a thousand extension steps before hitting a corner.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few scalar variables.

a.i: Extend the ray as a straight line through unfolded rooms. It reaches a corner after traveling n = p/g room-widths horizontally and m = q/g room-heights vertically, where g = gcd(p, q). If n is even the final wall is the left one (receptor 0 or 1); otherwise the right one (receptor 2). If m is even the corner is on the bottom (receptor 0); otherwise the top (receptor 1 or 2). Combining parities gives the answer directly.
s: Let m = (p/g) % 2 (vertical room count) and n = (q/g) % 2 (horizontal room count).
If m == 1 and n == 1, the ray ends at the top-right corner: return 2.
If m == 1 and n == 0, it ends at the top-left corner: return 1.
Otherwise (m == 0, n == 1) it ends at the bottom-left corner: return 0.
a.t: O(log(min(p, q))) — dominated by the Euclidean gcd computation.
a.sp: O(1) — constant extra space (recursion depth for gcd is logarithmic but negligible).

w: In an interview, mention the unfolding idea first — it shows geometric insight — then present the parity/GCD solution as the optimal answer; the simulation is only worth coding if you're unsure of the parity logic. Common pitfalls: forgetting that both p and q must be divided by their gcd before checking parity (e.g., p=4, q=2 reduces to 2×1, giving receptor 2, not 0); mixing up which receptor sits on which corner (0 bottom-left, 1 top-left, 2 top-right); and assuming the ray can loop forever — the guarantee that it meets a receptor means q/p in lowest terms has coprime numerator and denominator, so it always terminates. Follow-ups might ask for the number of reflections before hitting a receptor (it is m + n − 2 using the reduced counts) or generalization to rectangular rooms.
